**The meaning of the hadith**
In this hadith there is one of these scenes, told by Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, may Allah be pleased with him. He was standing in the row on the day of the Battle of Badr, which took place between the Muslims and the idolaters of Quraysh in the second year after the Hijrah. He looked to his right and to his left and found two young boys from the Ansar, and he wished he were standing between two men tougher and stronger than them, because a grown man is more patient in battle and of more use to the fighter beside him … Before long, Abd al-Rahman saw Abu Jahl moving about among the people, going back and forth among his disbelieving people and not staying in one place. So he pointed him out to them and told them that this was the Abu Jahl they had asked about. They rushed at him with their swords, that is, they hurried to strike him with their swords until they killed him. Then they went to the Prophet ﷺ and told him that they had killed Abu Jahl … He said to them, "You both killed him," only to comfort the heart of the other one, since he had a share in the killing and in the great reward that comes from it, even though there was a difference between them in who came first and whose blow had more effect.

The hadith shows that a person may keep the good he intends hidden from others, for fear that someone will beat him to it.

And it shows that no one should be looked down on; for some of those who are thought too young for a task may be greater than people imagine, and more deserving of that task.

📖 From the Hadith Encyclopedia — Dorar.net.

**Talk with your child**
1. What did Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, may Allah be pleased with him, wish when he saw the two boys to his right and to his left? And what did he learn about them by the end of the day?
2. Why did each of the two Mu'adhs ask about Abu Jahl? And why did each ask Abd al-Rahman secretly, without his friend hearing?
3. Why did the Prophet ﷺ say, "You both killed him"? And does the story mean that a child should hit someone who does wrong? (No; this was fighting in a battle against an attacking army. Standing up for what is right in our lives is done with a good word, telling the grown-ups, and standing by the one who is wronged.)

**This week's exercise**
Every day this week your child steps forward to do a good deed that others hold back from: being the first to say salam, getting to a job at home before being asked, or standing up with a kind word for a classmate who is being made fun of. And they tell you about one of them.
